# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Work finish

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). Detail: this skill's `references/closing.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. Check that the result approval is recorded. Not recorded: show the result, the gaps, and the evidence, and ask. "Ship it" or "mark it done" from the owner after he has seen the result counts as the approval; record it with his words. Each sub-item needs its own result approval: the owner's approval of the parent does not cover it.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect 'Result approved; work-finish continues.'`
2. Repository work: commit the item's files by name on its branch (no `Co-Authored-By` line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line), push it, open the pull request (description through `unslop`, no AI credit), and set the pull request stage. Merge through `merge-and-clean-up` when the owner approves the merge, or when `DECISIONS.md` records a standing merge instruction and the `acceptance-checker` agent found no blocking issue on that exact head. With no remote, a local merge (`git merge --ff-only <branch>` in the main checkout) follows the same approval: still set the pull request stage, and say "No remote: merged locally into <branch>." in a history note. The fast-forward fails when the default branch moved on after the item's branch was made (for example another item's local merge): merge the default branch into the item's branch in its worktree (`git merge <default-branch>`), run the item's checks again (under a standing merge instruction the `acceptance-checker` checks the new head), then run the fast-forward again. A merge that stops on a conflict is committed with a message you write, never `git commit --no-edit` (it keeps the "# Conflicts:" lines). In Codex, `git add`, `git commit`, `git merge`, `git push`, `git worktree remove`, and `git branch -d` need the owner's approval and escalated permissions (`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason), because the sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only: say in one line what each does before Codex asks. Refused without asking: show him the exact command and ask him to approve it or run it in a terminal.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 12-pr-and-push`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'No remote: merged locally into main.' --effect 'No pull request; no deployment.'`
3. Deployment, when the item needs one: set the deployment stage. Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` current and the item's folder in `delivery/deployment/` complete, then `sf-deploy-check`, then validate against the sandbox. Production deploys and production data loads are handed to the owner to run (`sf-data-change`).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 13-deployment`
4. Requirements baseline: set the spec update stage; read `requirements/AGENTS.md`; copy only delivered and approved behavior into the business area's one file in `requirements/`. A new area: copy `requirements/system-area-template/` to a folder named for the area and rename the copied `AREA-TEMPLATE.md` for it (for example `requirements/billing/BILLING.md`), so every area has the same layout; leave `system-area-template/` unchanged. Update the area's file in `system-guide/` when the verified structure changed (a new one is a copy of `system-guide/AREA-TEMPLATE.md` named for the area, for example `system-guide/billing.md`). Save both with `publish-docs`; with no remote it commits them on the default branch locally.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 14-spec-update`
5. Sub-items: list the open ones. Each is finished or cancelled on its own (with its own approval or reason), or moved when the owner asks (`work-organize`). A parent with open sub-items is finished only when the owner says so, with the `--allow-open-sub-items` finish command in step 8. Finishing a sub-item never finishes its parent.
   `toolkit work list --tree`
6. Memory: at most one `event` record through `memory-save`, only when the episode will matter later.
7. Before Done, check the item's files: every change the item made, including the `requirements/` and `system-guide/` updates from step 4, is committed and reached the default branch (or the owner said to leave it on the branch). `git status` in the main checkout shows none of them uncommitted. List the item's leftover worktrees and branches (`git worktree list`, `git branch --list '*<prefix>-<number>*'` with the item's id prefix in lower case, for example `'*wi-007*'`), compare each with the default branch, and offer to remove the ones already delivered; remove one only with the owner's yes, and never one that holds uncommitted work.
8. First set each finished Roadmap phase to Done, and in Overview bring Related items up to date (which sub-items delivered what), set Current position to "Done on <date>: <what shows it works>", and set Blockers to "None." (a blocker about a merge or branch that is now finished is stale). Then mark it Done with what shows it works (the command also closes Next action and Notes > Resume here, and says what still needs a note), and say whether the work reached the default branch. The second command is only for a result approval not yet recorded: `--quote` takes the owner's exact words approving the result. The third is only for a parent the owner said is done while sub-items are still open; quote his words in a history note. Take the item off the current focus "Now" list and out of "Next session starts with" (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus").
   `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'`
   `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>' --quote '<his exact words>'`
   `toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>' --allow-open-sub-items`
   `toolkit memory focus --json`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>`
9. Cancel: use the owner's words as the reason, and ask what happens to its open sub-items.
   `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`
10. Do not move or archive the folder unless the owner asks (`work-organize`). End the reply with the one question for the owner (the merge, the deploy, a leftover branch), or the exact words that continue ("Tell me the next thing to build.").

## Agents

- `acceptance-checker`: the independent check of the exact head before a merge under a standing merge instruction. Brief it as `work-check` does, and name the commit.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran. Without an independent check, a standing merge instruction does not apply: ask the owner.

## Rules

- Never mark Done without a recorded result approval or the owner's quoted words. The CLI requires `--by`, and `--quote` when no result approval is recorded.
- Never mark Done while the item's changes, or the requirements and system guide updates it made, are uncommitted.
- Approval of the result never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing. Each needs the owner's yes or a standing instruction recorded in the project.
- Agents never run production deploys or production data loads. Hand the owner the exact command and what to check afterwards; record his report in a history note.
- Only delivered and approved behavior goes into the area's file in `requirements/`. Approved but undelivered behavior is never written there as shipped.
- Stages that do not apply are skipped: work with no repository change has no pull request; work with no deployment has no deployment stage.
- No AI credit in commits, pull requests, or release notes.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Close the issue as completed, or as not planned for a cancel, as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

# Merge and clean up

Land one exact pull request, prove it merged, then remove only the workspace
that belonged to it. Merge and cleanup are one guarded workflow.

1. **Resolve the exact pull request** and map branches to worktrees. The local
   head branch must be at the pull request's head commit.
2. **Check the merge is allowed:** the owner's yes for this pull request, or a
   standing merge instruction recorded in `DECISIONS.md`.
3. **Preflight on GitHub:** open, not a draft, mergeable, reviews satisfied,
   required checks passed. "No checks reported" is not a failure.
4. **Merge-safety check:** after a fetch, compare
   `git diff --name-only origin/<default>...<branch>` with `git status` in the
   primary checkout. A file in both lists: stop and name it.
5. **Merge** with `gh pr merge <n> --squash --delete-branch` (no admin flags),
   then confirm the state is `MERGED`.
6. **Fast-forward the base checkout**, then remove only this pull request's
   worktree and branches.
7. **Add one history note** to the linked work item. Stage moves and Done stay
   with `work-finish`. Report the link, the merge commit, and the cleanup
   result.

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Codex: its sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only, so every Git write here (`git fetch`, `git pull`, `git push`, `git worktree remove`, `git branch -d`) and every `gh` call that needs the network needs the owner's approval and escalated permissions. Run each one as its own command with `sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated` and a one-line reason saying what it does; an approval without escalation still runs inside the sandbox and fails on `.git/index.lock`. When Codex refuses a command without asking ("approval required by policy"), stop, show the owner the exact command, and ask him to approve it in an interactive session or run it in a terminal.

No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): there is no pull request to merge, so this skill does not apply. Never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker. Say so in one line; the local merge of a work item's branch is `work-finish` step 2.

## Safety rules

- "Merge and clean up" is merge approval only when the target pull request is
  clear from a number, a URL, or the current branch. Ask when more than one
  could match.
- Read the project's `AGENTS.md` and `.claude/rules/` first. Project rules decide
  required checks, merge method, and who may merge.
- Never merge a draft, bypass branch protection, use an admin override,
  force-push, or ignore a failed required check.
- Never delete anything before GitHub reports the pull request as `MERGED`.
- Never delete the default branch, the base branch, an unrelated branch or
  worktree, a dirty worktree, or a branch with local commits that are not in the
  pull request head.
- List every worktree before and after cleanup. Unrelated ones stay.
- If any proof is missing, stop at the safe point and report exactly what
  remains.

## 1. Resolve the exact target

Take the repository and pull request from the number or URL. For "this PR",
resolve it from the current checkout:

```bash
git status -sb
git remote -v
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
gh pr view --json number,url,state,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefName,isCrossRepository,title,body
```

Record: repository owner and name, pull request number and URL, head branch and
head commit, base branch, the worktree holding the head branch (if any), the
worktree holding the base branch, and whether the head branch is in a fork. Map
branches to paths with:

```bash
git worktree list --porcelain
```

If the local head branch exists, its commit must equal `headRefOid` before you
promise it can be deleted. A different commit means local-only work exists: stop
and keep it.

Find the linked work item id: a head branch named like `claude/wi-007-<slug>`
(or `wi-007-<slug>`), or any branch containing `WI-007`, belongs to `WI-007`.
The id prefix is in lower case in a branch name, so `claude/tv2-007-<slug>`
belongs to `TV2-007`. Otherwise look for an id in the pull request title or
body. No id found: skip the history note in step 7.

## 2. Check the merge is allowed

The merge needs one of these:

- The owner's own yes for this pull request, in this conversation.
- A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project, recorded as a
  `DECISIONS.md` row that no later row replaces (the project's `AGENTS.md`
  says merges need the owner unless `DECISIONS.md` records one). Follow its
  conditions exactly (for example an independent review with no blocking
  findings on this exact head).

A work item that says its merge needs the owner's approval overrides a standing
instruction. When neither is present, stop and ask the owner. `work-finish`
asks for this approval; this skill only checks it.

## 3. Preflight

```bash
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner/repo> \
  --json number,title,state,isDraft,mergeable,mergeStateStatus,reviewDecision,statusCheckRollup,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefName,isCrossRepository,url
gh pr checks <number> --repo <owner/repo>
```

Merge only when the pull request is open and not a draft, GitHub reports it
mergeable, required reviews are satisfied, required checks passed, and the head
and base still match what step 1 recorded.

- Already merged: skip the merge, record its merge commit, and recheck that the
  head branch and commit match the workspace you plan to remove.
- Closed without merging: stop.
- `gh pr checks` exits nonzero when no checks exist. That means no configured
  check, not a failed one. Run any required local checks the project names, and
  say plainly when no automated check exists.
- Pending checks: wait only when the owner asked you to finish the merge.
- Failed checks: stop and report. Do not merge around them.

The head worktree must be clean before merging:

```bash
git -C <head-worktree> status --porcelain
```

Any output blocks cleanup. Do not stash or discard it.

## 4. Merge-safety check

Other sessions may have uncommitted work in the primary checkout. A merge that
changes the same files would collide with it. The primary checkout is the first
entry that `git worktree list` prints. Fetch first, so the comparison uses the
remote's default branch, not a local copy that may be behind:

```bash
git worktree list
git fetch origin
git diff --name-only origin/<default-branch>...<head-branch>
git -C <primary-checkout> status --porcelain
```

With no local head branch, use `origin/<head-branch>` in the diff. If any file
appears in both lists, stop. Name exactly those files and let the
owner decide whether to commit, stash, or wait. Do not touch the primary
checkout's changes.

## 5. Merge

Use the merge method the owner or the project requires. When neither says:
squash for a normal single-purpose branch; a merge commit when the commit
structure matters; ask when the choice would change history in a way that
matters.

```bash
gh pr merge <number> --repo <owner/repo> --squash --delete-branch
```

Replace `--squash` with the chosen method when needed. Leave out
`--delete-branch` for a pull request from a fork: that branch belongs to the
contributor. Never add an admin or protection-bypass flag. Then verify:

```bash
gh pr view <number> --repo <owner/repo> \
  --json state,mergedAt,mergeCommit,url,headRefName,headRefOid,baseRefName,isCrossRepository
```

Do not clean up unless `state` is `MERGED`.

## 6. Update the base checkout, then remove only the merged workspace

The worktree holding the base branch must be clean and on the expected branch:

```bash
git -C <base-worktree> fetch --prune origin
git -C <base-worktree> pull --ff-only
```

If it is dirty, on another branch, or cannot fast-forward, leave it untouched,
do no local cleanup from it, and report the blocker. Never reset, stash,
switch, or rebase it.

Recheck five proofs before removing anything:

1. GitHub reports this exact pull request merged.
2. The branch to remove is the pull request's head branch, not the base or
   default branch.
3. The worktree to remove is clean.
4. The local branch commit still equals the recorded head commit.
5. No other worktree uses that branch.

Run cleanup from the base worktree, never from inside the worktree being
removed:

```bash
git -C <base-worktree> worktree remove <head-worktree>
git -C <base-worktree> branch -d <head-branch>
git -C <base-worktree> worktree prune
```

A squash merge does not make the old branch commit part of the base, so
`git branch -d` can refuse even after a good merge. Use
`git branch -D <head-branch>` only when all five proofs still hold and that is
the only refusal. This is not permission to force-delete any other branch.

If GitHub did not delete the remote branch, delete it only when it is in the
same repository and belongs to this merged pull request:

```bash
git -C <base-worktree> push origin --delete <head-branch>
git -C <base-worktree> fetch --prune origin
```

Never try to delete a contributor's fork branch.

## 7. Work item note and report

When the project has `.toolkit.json` and step 1 found a work item id, add one
history note:

```text
toolkit work history <id> --note 'Merged pull request <number> as <merge commit>'
```

For a GitHub Issues or Jira tracker, `toolkit work` exits with code 3 and
prints the path of that tracker's written instructions; follow them to add the
same note to the issue. Do not change the stage or mark anything Done: that is
`work-finish`'s job, after the owner approves the result. Do not invent a work
item when none exists.

Verify: the pull request is merged; the base checkout matches its upstream and
is clean; the head branch is gone locally and on the remote; its worktree is
gone; every unrelated worktree remains.

End with the pull request link, the merge commit, the final base state, the
cleanup result, and whether the history note was saved ("Not saved" first when
it failed). The last line is the one question for the owner (a remaining
action he must take), or the exact words that continue ("Say 'finish WI-007'
and I'll close the work item.").

item.aggregated_output:
# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`
names the file when a rule matters for a step.

This file is `references/conventions.md` in the work plugin's own folder. From
a skill's `SKILL.md` it is two folders up: `skills/work-on/SKILL.md` and
`references/conventions.md` share the plugin folder. In Codex the plugin
folder is the installed copy, for example
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/`, so this file is
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/references/conventions.md`.

Rules that are easy to miss:

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, as its own command, in both hosts (below).
- Never change a work item with a script (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`).
  Use `toolkit work edit --section` or `--label`, or the file edit tool for
  body text. The hooks refuse the script, so it only wastes a step.
- Text goes on standard input in Claude Code and in single quotes or a
  `mktemp -d` file in Codex, never in double quotes and never at a fixed name
  such as `/tmp/wi001.md` ("Text in a command", below).
- Ask the owner in the reply text. Never ask through a question tool (such as
  Codex's `request_user_input`): he may never see it, and the reply must hold
  the question.
- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never
  report a refused or failed fetch as a blocker.
- End every reply to the owner with the one question he must answer, or with
  the exact words that continue the work ("Say 'keep going' and I'll start the
  build."). Never end on "The next step is ..." with nothing for him to do.
- Keep the current focus current when an item's stage or next step changes
  ("The current focus", below).

## Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file in `agents/` carries
its own writing rules.

## Opening another skill

- Claude Code: use the Skill tool with the skill's name, for example
  `work-requirements`.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path shown in the skill list,
  then follow it.
- Say the handover in one line, for example "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`. The
  agent-led delivery offer is the one exception: only `work-delegate` makes
  the offer and records its answer.

## Running `toolkit` commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion,
  Hindsight, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and `.memory/` from a
  worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong cause. Codex matches
  its command rule against the plain command.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc, "Text in a command" below).
- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field.
- Exit codes: `0` done; `1` error; `2` validation failure (fix what it names
  and run it again); `3` not supported for this tracker or memory backend
  (follow [trackers.md](trackers.md)); `4` not a Toolkit V2 project (open
  `project-setup`).
- "saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first line that differs. Lead the
  reply to the owner with "Saved but not verified", say which line, and read
  the item back to judge it.

## Changing a work item

- Change a work item only through `toolkit work` commands. This keeps the
  local tracker and Notion the same, and it keeps the CLI's record of what it
  wrote. A value the agent changes by hand looks like an owner edit to the
  CLI.
- Find a file only with the command below. Never build a path by hand: the
  owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --path
  ```

- To change one section of the body, read it, change only what needs to
  change, and write the whole section back. The new text is the same text the
  read printed for that heading, with your changes. Leave out the section's
  fill-in guide comment (`<!-- ... -->`) once the section holds real content.
  `<file>` below is `-` (standard input) in Claude Code ("Text in a command").

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --section "<heading>"
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file <file>
  ```

- To add one row to a table section (Open Questions, Recent History), use
  `--append-row` with the full Markdown table row. A new question takes the
  next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions section first and add one to
  the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is none).

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |'
  ```

- Frontmatter values change only through `toolkit work set`, `approve`,
  `design`, `move`, `finish`, and `cancel`. Never edit frontmatter by hand.
- A title is the owner's call. A new item's title uses the owner's own words
  for the request. When you shorten them or choose another, say the title in
  one line in the reply ("I started WI-003, 'Write a short project brief'.").
  To retitle an item, say the new title to him in one line before
  `toolkit work set <id> --title`, and never retitle an item quietly.
- Never hand-edit `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md` or
  `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`. The hooks refuse it.
- Never write a work item record from the shell (`cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`,
  `cp`, or a script) and never change its frontmatter with a file edit. The
  hooks refuse both, because they would skip the approval gates.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still prints "Saved". So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Write an apostrophe inside them as `'\''`, for example
  `--note 'Owner'\''s words: "ship it"'`. Never use double quotes for text.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere. Claude Code
  refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary folder there could never be
  deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file - <<'EOF'
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text,
  make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d` (its name is unique, so
  two sessions or two projects never share a file), write the file in it with
  the file edit tool (`apply_patch`), run the `toolkit` command alone with the
  file's full path, and delete the file and the folder right after the command
  succeeds (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner
  anything. Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell
  command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  ```

- Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`: every project
  starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this item.
- Never leave draft files inside `.work-items/`: a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped
  file there confuses the design lookup.

## Section names in `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` uses. Every tracker uses the same body: the
project's `.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`, copied from the model
project.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | Phases `P1`, `P2` with Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | Tasks `P1-T01` with Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: change or decision, effect on the work |
| `Open Questions` | `Q-01` rows: question, affects, status, decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status, Starting request, Agreed goal, Active requirements `R-01`, Acceptance |
| `Notes` | Decisions and context, Resume here, Solution options and considerations |

The frontmatter fields are `id`, `title`, `type`, `stage`, `status`, `parent`,
`waiting_on`, `priority`, `delivery`, `requirements_approved`, `design`,
`result_approved`, and `updated`. Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

## Section names in `DESIGN.md`

The design has one shape in every tracker (`DESIGN.md` beside a local item,
the "Solution Design" page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub
or Jira). The CLI writes its frontmatter: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what the design leaves to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, and the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C) with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage (Build or reuse, Why it meets the requirement, How to check it), Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow, Components and responsibilities, Data, access, and integration details, Edge cases and failure behavior, Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep the headings exactly as the template has them, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`.

## Saving what the owner says

Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
unanswered question is also information to save. Open decisions do not delay
saving answers that are already settled.

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Requirements` section (the `R-xx` block and Acceptance) | The new meaning, and Status `Refining` until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer (`owner` or a name) |
| Answer or decision about this item | The existing question row, the affected section, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, deliverable, done when, depends on |
| Useful context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to; it is not a requirement |
| A lasting fact, preference, or lesson | Project memory, through `memory-save` | One record |

- Check the item and memory before asking the owner a question again.
- When sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Do not pick the
  convenient answer.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.

## Reporting a failed save

- A write failed: lead with "Not saved", name what was not saved and where it
  should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified".
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## When to add a history note

Add one `toolkit work history <id> --note '<text>' --effect '<what it changes>'`
when (without `--effect`, the row says which skill continues the item):

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who, and do not claim you
  checked it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

Record the owner's meaning briefly. Do not add reasons, scope, or certainty he
did not give. Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs,
or small edits.

A note that quotes the owner's approval ("Owner's words: ...") right after an
approval or a `waiting_on` change gets its own `--effect` that says what the
answer changes ("Result approved; work-finish continues."). Without it, the
row's default effect is worked out from the item before the change and can
name the wrong next step.

## Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask the owner for an approval or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
- `toolkit work approve` sets `waiting_on` from `owner` to `none`, because the
  owner just answered. After the approval, set it to `agent` when the agent
  continues. After the owner answers his last open question on the item, set
  it back the same way: `agent` when the agent can continue, `none` when
  nothing waits. Keep `owner` only while another question for him on that
  item is still open.

  ```text
  toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent
  ```

- An item left at `owner` stays in the briefing and in
  `toolkit work decisions`, and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of
  its next stage.

## The current focus

The current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) is the first thing the next session
reads. Its "Now" section names work item ids and titles, never their status;
its "Next session starts with" section says where to resume. A line there that
names a step already done misleads every later session.

When an item's stage changes, or its next step changes to something the focus
does not say, read the focus and check two things before the reply ends:

- "Now" lists the item (id and title only). Add it when it is missing; take
  it off when the item is Done or Cancelled.
- "Next session starts with" does not name a step that is done or no longer
  next. Replace that line with the item's real next step, in one line that
  points at the item ("Continue WI-012 from its Resume here: build P1.").

Also drop a setup step under "Waiting on the owner" once `toolkit doctor` no
longer reports it. Change the "Last updated" line (date, source, who) and keep
the `# Current focus` title line. Leave every other line as it is. Save the
whole text back with the version you read, so another session's change is not
lost (`--expect` refuses a stale save with exit code 2: read it again and
redo the change). Claude Code passes the text on standard input.

```text
toolkit memory focus --json
toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>
```

Skip the save when nothing in the focus is wrong. The work item itself stays
the record of where the item stands.

## Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`, for example "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in. Work it out from the record.
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item is waiting for.
  Blocked is not a status.

## Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move a folder, drag a Notion card,
change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, adds a "Changed by hand" history row,
and reports it. Never undo it. When a hand change skips a gate (a build item
moved past stage 03 without approved requirements, or Done without a recorded
result approval), ask the owner about it as a question.

The session briefing lists these changes under "Changes found in the
tracker", and every `toolkit work` command prints the ones it finds. Tell the
owner each one in one line ("You renamed WI-002's folder to help-option; I'll
use the new path.") before other work. The CLI writes the history rows for a
hand move itself: "Moved by hand", "Folder renamed by hand", or "Parent
changed in Notion by hand" on the item, and "Sub-item ... moved out" or
"moved here" on the parents it left and joined. Add a note only for what the
CLI cannot know, such as the owner's reason.

## Branches and worktrees

- An item's code work happens in its own worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, the form the project's
  `shared-repository-work.md` rule uses. `<prefix>` is the item's own id
  prefix in lower case: `wi` for `WI-007`, `tv2` for `TV2-007`, `acme` for
  `ACME-007`. For WI-007:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`.
  The briefing ties a worktree to its item by the item id in the branch name,
  so a branch named `wi-001-...` for `TV2-001` is not linked to it.
- Never commit `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. They are Git-ignored and live in
  the main checkout.
- No AI credit anywhere: not in commits, pull requests, comments, or files.
  A commit message never carries a `Co-Authored-By` line naming an AI or a
  "Generated with" line. Stage files by name; never `git add -A`, `git add .`,
  or `git commit -a`.
- Codex: its sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only, so `git add`, `git commit`,
  `git worktree add` and `remove`, `git merge`, `git branch -d`, `git fetch`,
  and `git push` cannot run inside it. The project's
  `.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one.
  - Run each Git write as its own command and ask for escalated permissions:
    set `sandbox_permissions` to `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason
    that says what the command does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own
    branch."). An approval without escalation still runs the command inside
    the sandbox, where it fails on `.git/index.lock`.
  - Tell the owner in one line what the command does before Codex asks.
  - Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy, but
    AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
    step, show the owner the exact command, ask him to approve it in an
    interactive session or to run it in a terminal, and set the item waiting
    on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.
  - Never work around it: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
    `.git/`, no building on the default branch instead of the item's branch.
- The project's shared-repository rule runs `git fetch origin` before the
  first edit. When `git remote` prints nothing, the project has no remote:

name: memory-save
description: 'Saves, corrects, or forgets one lasting fact in the project''s memory, or sends it to the record where it belongs. Use when the owner says "remember this", "from now on", "forget that", or "remind me" with no time given, corrects the agent, or a hook says a save is due.'
---

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion). Text: one-line values (`--description`, `--source`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)` and drop that text. A record body, the focus, or the glossary: in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--body-file -` or `--set-file -`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), never through a file; in Codex give it in single quotes (`--body '<text>'`, `--text '<text>'`), or write a file with the file edit tool in a new folder made with `mktemp -d`, run the `toolkit` command alone with that file, and delete the file and the folder right after. Never write the file and run the command in one shell command, and never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate. The save command checks too: when memory already has a record with the same key or a very similar description or text, it saves nothing, exits with code 2, and lists those records. Read each one with the second command below, which prints its `version` field. The same fact: save that record's type and slug again with `--expect <version>`, which updates it (the first 12 characters of the version are enough; for a record with the same key, the command's own fix line already gives them). A newer fact that replaces it: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. A different fact: say why in one line and save again with `--allow-similar`. Never add `--allow-similar` without reading the listed records.
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. An unanswered "Save to memory?" (his next message does not answer it, or the session is ending) is not dropped: save it as a proposal (`--proposal`, never with an approver). A proposal is not a fact: search leaves it out, the agent does not rely on it, and the decision list shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it through `work-decide`.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body with the model's bold labels, each starting its own paragraph: `**Remember:**`, `**Why:**` (the owner's reason in his words, or "Not stated by the owner."; never a reason you inferred), `**How to apply:**`, `**Evidence and limits:**` (the source and an absolute date), `**Related memories:**` (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), `**Authoritative records:**`. Never write them as `## headings`. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again, with `--expect <version>` (the `version` field of the step 2 read), updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. A better name or a type that matches the content: rename it; links to it are repaired. The first form is for the owner's approval (his words or his yes); the second for a routine save in `trusted` mode; the third for an unanswered proposal; the fourth updates a record read in step 2. `<file>` is `-` in Claude Code.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>'`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --proposal`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus with its version, change it, write the whole text back. The model's format: the `# Current focus` title line, a "Last updated" line (date, source, who), and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status; keep the title and the date line (the CLI adds them when missing, but without the source and who). Drop a setup step under "Waiting on the owner" once doctor no longer reports it. On a new project remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus --json`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." (a proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."). A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses. End the reply with the question still waiting for him, if there is one, or those exact words.
   `toolkit memory get <key>`
   `toolkit doctor`

## Changing the approval mode

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.
- Switch to trusted, or back to onboarding:
  `toolkit config set memory.approval trusted`
  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

## Hook reminders

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.
- The Stop hook blocks once when a keep phrase had no save this turn. Save it, or tell the owner in one line why it belongs elsewhere and where it went.

## Proposals and declined saves

- A proposal saved in step 3 waits for the owner's yes or no; `work-decide` asks him. His answer in this chat also settles it: yes approves it (a current record with him as the approver), no rejects it (the proposal is deleted).
  `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
  `toolkit memory reject <key>`
- When the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it (a saved proposal: reject it). Do not put the rejected fact in the current focus, the glossary, or another record, and never propose it again under other words. If his words give a general rule about what to save, save only that rule, as a `feedback` record.
- Several independent things can be grouped into one save. Never run two saves against the same record or the index at once.

## Backend notes

- Built-in `.memory/`: never edit the files by hand; the CLI writes them and rebuilds `.memory/MEMORY.md`. The folder opens as an Obsidian vault. When a record is renamed, merged, retired, or deleted, the CLI repairs the links in other notes and names each note it changed; read that report (`references/record-format.md`, "Links between memories").
- Hindsight or Notion unreachable: the save fails with "Not saved". Keep the text, tell the owner in one line, and retry later in the session.
- Undo a retire:
  `toolkit memory restore <key>`
# Local project memory

Keep future sessions oriented without turning every conversation into lasting memory. This folder is the project's built-in memory store and can be opened directly as an Obsidian vault. Active topics stay flat; filenames and YAML types agree. Git ignores this folder, so back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>`.

## Read and route

- Read `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` at startup; the session briefing includes it. Read `MEMORY.md` as a short index, then open relevant topics. Check dates, scope, and the current source before acting on a remembered claim.
- Read `memory-criteria.md` before selecting or changing memory. It holds the default eligibility rules; the `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy and the onboarding or trusted mode. Use the terminology glossary for project language, including distinct meanings across systems.
- Link related notes inside this vault with relative Markdown links, such as `[account model](project_account_model.md)`. Obsidian shows backlinks to a note from the notes that link to it; a second reverse link is optional. Link only when the relationship helps retrieval, and check that the target exists. Keep tracker URLs and paths outside `.memory/` as source references rather than vault links.
- Keep current tasks and owner-mentioned to-dos in `CURRENT_FOCUS.md`, naming work items by ID. Keep full tasks, status, requirements, history, and the work item's design together in the chosen tracker; verified system behavior in the System Guide; procedures in instructions or skills; and raw outside sources in their source folders.

## Curate

- Use a coherent topic file such as `project_account_data_model.md`. Allowed prefixes and matching `metadata.type` values are `user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, and `event`. `project_topic_template.md` is a seed, not a saved memory. Keep one related topic per file and aim for a quick read.
- Record source and date, status, scope, the durable point, why it matters, and how to apply it. Keep uncertainty explicit. Preserve extra YAML fields written by a host or imported record.
- Search for an existing topic before creating one (`toolkit memory find`). Correct, merge, or supersede in place where possible. Mark obsolete claims in both file text and index; do not leave an archived item reading as currently open.
- When renaming, merging, archiving, or deleting a topic, inspect links from other memory notes and repair any affected links, saving each repaired note with `toolkit memory save`. Do not leave a link pointing at a former active location.
- `toolkit memory save`, `retire`, and `restore` rebuild `MEMORY.md`; run `toolkit memory reindex` after any other topic change. The index holds one short link per active topic, not the content itself. Keep it below the configured budget.
- Keep `CURRENT_FOCUS.md` under 50 lines by replacing stale sections, not appending, and write it with `toolkit memory focus --set-file`. Do not remove an unresolved owner to-do solely to meet that limit.
- Keep the glossary broad through sourced real terms, aliases, and system-specific meanings, and write it with `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. Do not invent definitions.

## Authority and completion

- Save through the `memory-save` skill, which holds the approval policy for onboarding and trusted mode. An explicit request to remember or correct is authorization for that specific change.
- Ask before ambiguous, bulk, or irreversible deletion of unique content. Only the owner can change the mode.
- A rejected candidate is not saved to another memory, a criteria example, the glossary, or a pending queue. Record only the general selection lesson, as a `feedback` memory, if the owner gave one.
- The main agent writes this folder only with `toolkit memory` commands, for example `save`, `retire`, `focus`, `glossary`, and `reindex` (`toolkit memory --help` lists them all). They lock the folder, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index. Never run parallel writers against the same topic.
- Read back changes with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor` before reporting success. Memory work does not edit requirements, work-item status, designs, deployments, or source code.
# Memory criteria

This file is the project-specific selection policy: what is worth keeping in lasting memory. The approval policy, including onboarding and trusted mode, is in the `memory-save` skill, which saves with `toolkit memory save`. When the owner corrects what is worth saving, save the correction as a `feedback` memory with `memory-save`, as a general rule, without copying the rejected memory. Those `feedback` memories override this page.

## Default test for lasting memory

Save a topic when it concerns this project, has a credible source, would matter in a future session, would be costly or unreliable to reconstruct, and has no better maintained owner. Prefer updating an existing topic. A short pointer to an authoritative record can qualify when future sessions would otherwise miss that record.

| Type and filename | Usually worth retaining | Route or reject instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_<topic>.md` | Relevant role, responsibility, working preference, or communication need the owner stated | Personal judgments, irrelevant biography, private details |
| `feedback_<topic>.md` | Repeated or standing correction to how the agent should work; confirmed selection lesson | One-off irritation, a rejected fact restated as policy, an instruction already in `AGENTS.md` |
| `project_<topic>.md` | Durable project constraint, rationale, technical landmark, or proven costly fix | A decision for the whole project (`DECISIONS.md`), code summary, schema copy, active ticket status, accepted requirement or design body |
| `reference_<topic>.md` | Hard-to-rediscover route to a source, system, dashboard, or decision record, with why to open it | Entire outside page or a path already obvious in `PROJECT.md` or the project map |
| `event_<topic>.md` | Significant project episode: what was done, what resulted, and where the output lives | Routine edit, tool call, raw error, daily progress log |

## Working context is different

`CURRENT_FOCUS.md` holds what is happening now: active work item IDs, what waits on the owner with no work item, untracked to-dos, and where the next session starts. It can change often. Keep a work item's detailed tasks and status in that item. Do not turn every open task into lasting memory. Do not discard an unresolved owner to-do merely to shorten the file.

## Never save as lasting memory

- Secrets, credentials, sensitive personal data, transcripts, scratch reasoning, raw logs, dropped guesses, or unsupported claims.
- A fact the same change already places in the authoritative file, unless a small route to that file is genuinely needed.
- Live status, pending approval, unshipped requirements, procedure steps, code restatements, or a current-system explanation that the code/System Guide owns.
- A rejected candidate under a new name or wider wording. A rejection stands until the owner changes it.

## Backup

This folder is Git-ignored. Back it up with `toolkit memory export --to <folder outside this project>` and restore a fresh clone with `toolkit memory import --from <that folder>`. Linked worktrees resolve to one vault in the main checkout. A fresh clone or machine needs its memory restored before the agent treats an empty index as evidence that no memory exists.
